subChunks.title: The Grand Commission
subChunks.hookHtml:
Four sections. One page. Everything you have learned — sticky headers, gradient backgrounds, gradient text, coloured shadows, the group pattern, ring highlights, multi-breakpoint grids, object-cover, absolute positioning — converges here.

The guild is watching. Grand Archmage Solomon himself will review the final page. This is the moment that separates a practitioner from an expert.

The Grand Commission is open. Demonstrate your mastery.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Grand Archmage Solomon: "You have learned every technique this commission requires. The gradient background. The gradient text. The sticky header. The group pattern. The ring. The status dot. The responsive grids. Individually they are tools. Together, assembled with judgment and precision, they are a product. You will now assemble them."

Lyra the Scribe: "I have prepared the HTML skeleton. Every section is present. Every semantic class name is applied. But the Tailwind utilities are stripped. You must restore them from memory and understanding, not from copying. The starter code has comments at each section reminding you what is required. Trust your knowledge."

What this challenge tests

This is not a recall exercise — it is a synthesis exercise. You will encounter moments where you must choose between similar approaches:

  • Sticky vs fixed for the header — you know the answer
  • Ring vs border for the featured card — you know which affects layout and which does not
  • hidden lg:block vs lg:hidden block for the hero visual — the order of mobile-first matters
  • text-transparent bg-clip-text vs just a coloured heading — you know which creates the gradient text effect

Working methodically

Work section by section. Start with the header — it is the simplest. Then the hero. Then services. Then team. Do not jump around. Each section is self-contained.

Deploying your commission

CodePen (fastest — 2 minutes)

  1. Go to codepen.io, create a free account, click + New Pen
  2. Paste your completed HTML into the HTML panel — the CDN script is already in the starter code
  3. Click Save — your page is live at a codepen.io URL

GitHub Pages (portfolio-grade — 5 minutes)

  1. Create a new public GitHub repo named arcane-guild
  2. Add your HTML as index.html, commit to main
  3. Go to Settings → Pages → Source: main branch → Save
  4. Your site is live at https://your-username.github.io/arcane-guild/

Grand Archmage Solomon: "A craftsperson without a portfolio is invisible. Every future employer will ask to see your work. This URL is evidence — of your taste, your precision, and your craft. Guard it. Maintain it. Point to it with pride."

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Apply all Tailwind classes to the complete Arcane Guild page. The HTML structure is provided with all four sections. Your task is to restore every class from TWL1 through TWL4:

  1. Header — sticky frosted-glass header with responsive navigation
  2. Hero — dark gradient section with two-column layout and gradient text
  3. Services — three-card grid with group hover effects and featured ring
  4. Team — four-column grid with circular avatars and status dots

The comments in the starter code tell you which classes each section requires. This is a full-page synthesis — every technique from this chapter must be applied correctly for all tests to pass.

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: The final act of every commission is delivery. Take your completed Grand Commission page and deploy it to a live public URL — this is your portfolio artefact. Deploy to CodePen or GitHub Pages, verify the sticky header, gradient text, card hover effects, and responsive grid all work. Then share your URL.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: You have just built a complete multi-section landing page with Tailwind. The client now wants to change the brand colour from indigo to violet across the entire site. Describe two different approaches: one that works for the current codebase (utility classes throughout), and one that would have been the ideal architectural choice from the start. Which approach would you recommend if you were starting fresh today?

questions.prompt: A non-technical client asks: 'Why do some classes start with lg: or md: or sm:?' Give the clearest, most accurate explanation.
options: They are responsive breakpoint prefixes — the class only applies when the screen is at least that wide. Tailwind is mobile-first, so unprefixed classes apply at all sizes, and prefixed classes activate at and above that breakpoint.
They are browser prefixes for specific browser compatibility, similar to -webkit- or -moz-
They are media query shortcuts that reduce the size of the full Tailwind stylesheet
They are optional style layers that activate only in production builds
questions.answer: They are responsive breakpoint prefixes — the class only applies when the screen is at least that wide. Tailwind is mobile-first, so unprefixed classes apply at all sizes, and prefixed classes activate at and above that breakpoint.
questions.explanation: Tailwind uses a mobile-first approach: grid-cols-1 applies at all screen sizes; md:grid-cols-3 overrides it at screens 768px and wider; lg:grid-cols-4 overrides again at 1024px and wider. Reading a responsive class string, always start from the unprefixed value (the mobile default) and then read each prefix as 'at this size and above, switch to this.'

questions.prompt: The full-page layout has a two-column hero grid (lg:grid-cols-2) with the right column using hidden lg:block. On a 900px screen (between md and lg), what does the layout look like?
options: A single column with only the text content visible — the hero visual is hidden because lg is not yet active
A two-column layout with both columns visible
A two-column layout but the visual column is transparent
An error — grid-cols-1 and lg:grid-cols-2 cannot coexist
questions.answer: A single column with only the text content visible — the hero visual is hidden because lg is not yet active
questions.explanation: At 900px, the lg: breakpoint (1024px) has not yet activated. So grid-cols-1 is still in effect (single column), and hidden lg:block means the visual column is still display: none. The visitor sees only the text content. This is the intentional mobile/tablet layout — the decorative card would clutter a narrower screen.

questions.prompt: A colleague reviews the finished page and says: 'The nav bar disappears on mobile — that's a bug.' You explain it is intentional. What is the complete explanation?
options: The nav uses hidden md:flex — it is deliberately hidden on screens below 768px because a full horizontal nav does not work on small screens. The correct fix is to add a mobile hamburger menu with md:hidden, not to make the desktop nav visible on mobile.
The nav uses display:none on mobile because Tailwind automatically hides navs on mobile for performance reasons
It is a bug — all navigation should always be visible regardless of screen size
The nav is hidden because md:flex does not work without a flex parent container
questions.answer: The nav uses hidden md:flex — it is deliberately hidden on screens below 768px because a full horizontal nav does not work on small screens. The correct fix is to add a mobile hamburger menu with md:hidden, not to make the desktop nav visible on mobile.
questions.explanation: Hiding the horizontal desktop nav on mobile is correct responsive design practice. A four-link horizontal nav bar on a 375px iPhone screen either overflows, wraps awkwardly, or forces tiny text. The production solution is to pair hidden md:flex (desktop nav) with a hamburger button that uses md:hidden (mobile nav toggle) — showing the mobile nav in a dropdown or slide-out drawer.
